method: Same-agent English/Marathi close reading and reverse paraphrase of reducibility propositions, exercises and Turing-reducibility digression, with formula, macro, token, label and reference parity after one documented type projection. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed.
scope: Transitivity of many-one reducibility; downward preservation of c.e. and computable sets; complement and characteristic-function exercises; Turing versus many-one, Karp and Cook reductions.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: A≤_m B means A is no harder than B. The relation is transitive: composing an A-to-B reduction f with a B-to-C reduction g yields an A-to-C reduction. The exercise asks for the same claim using the source's composition macro.
samples.checks: All relation directions, labels, composite macro and problem instruction are preserved.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: If A≤_m B, then c.e. of B implies c.e. of A and computability of B implies computability of A. With B as the domain of partial g, A is the domain of g composed after f. If B is computable, B and its complement are c.e.; f also reduces the complement of A to the complement of B, so both A and its complement are c.e. Alternatively χ_A equals χ_B composed after f.
samples.checks: The downward direction, partial-domain equation, both complement applications, two theorem references and characteristic-function identity remain exact.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The first exercise asks to prove that a reduction also reduces complementary sets. The second asks for χ_A=χ_B∘f on all naturals for a total A-to-B many-one reduction f:N→N. The frozen exercise instead types f:A→B, inconsistent with the preceding definition and insufficient outside A.
samples.checks: The complement sets, target identity and corrected global function type are present. OLCMP-022 documents the bounded correction and reader note.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The non-c.e. complement of K_0 cannot many-one reduce to c.e. K_0, yet an oracle for K_0 can answer complement queries. Turing reducibility permits a computable procedure to ask B questions, whereas many-one asks one answer-preserving question. Computable B still yields computable A under Turing reduction, but c.e. B need not yield c.e. A. The chapter uses many-one; polynomial-time analogues are Karp and Cook reducibility.
samples.checks: The cited non-c.e. result, oracle distinction, one-question yes/no preservation, computability versus c.e. contrast and named complexity analogues are retained.
